title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
description: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in th
body: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools   - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".Some officials say it originated in Taiwan. A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

schema.headline: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools

title: Famed ship SS United States deliberately sunk off Florida coast to become a reef
description: Figure caption, Watch: Moment historic ship sinks off the coast of FloridaByAna FaguyUpdated 12 November 2026 04:03 GMTA ship that was once the fastes
body: Figure caption, Watch: Moment historic ship sinks off the coast of FloridaByAna FaguyUpdated 12 November 2026 04:03 GMTA ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic has intentionally been sunk off the coast of Florida, turning into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it was added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, with a land-based museum detailing the ship's history also planned. Image source, Getty ImagesBefore its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities between the US and Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969. A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it was sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives. Figure caption, This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artificial reef.Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, SS United States in the 1950'sInstead, it sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out. The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the liner - said she was glad that the story of the SS United States would live on. "[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

schema.headline: Famed ship SS United States deliberately sunk off Florida coast to become a reef

title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports. CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal. Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade. While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials. "After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents. Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area. In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans. The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year. Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard. The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

schema.headline: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats

title: Kampala school deaths: Ugandan police investigate suspected poisoning
description: Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.The fo
body: Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations. According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil. Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital. Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from. The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

schema.headline: Kampala school deaths: Ugandan police investigate suspected poisoning

title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
description: A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arr
body: A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires. His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded. Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained. Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín. However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.A nationwide manhunt is now under way. Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office. Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s. Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

schema.headline: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony

title: Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
description: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacemen
body: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government.Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid.His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto.Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president."[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia"."He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said.Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated."No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.The Supreme Court ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi said.Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.But tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.Last week, authorities arrested several senior officials, including presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation to Prabowo - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.But neither man has confirmed the rift. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Jokowi said he still supported Prabowo's leadership. Jokowi also said Gibran's resignation was part of "political dynamics" and he had told his son "the position was temporary".All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The  free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.Across the country, students and activists have staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

schema.headline: Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying

title: Ebola in DR Congo: Millions of dollars going missing as virus spreads, MSF warns
description: Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical cha
body: Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.A report from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.It added that in some cases ambulances had run out of fuel.More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.The Congolese health minister echoed these concerns, saying that aid agencies were required to provide details of their work so the ministry could provide oversight but that only 22% had done so."Our requirement is clear: transparency must be total. The response relies on a single plan, a single budget, and a single coordination," Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said on X., externalIn its report, external, the charity said: "Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets."It also mentioned Ebola monitoring "surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground"."Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable," said MSF president Javid Abdelmoneim.One important way of stopping Ebola from spreading is contact tracing - finding all those people who had come into contact with an infected person and putting them into isolation."Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic," MSF said, adding that two-thirds of deaths were occurring in communities not treatment centres.According to British epidemiologist Neil Ferguson, more than half of the cases are going undetected, meaning the outbreak is likely to last another year, reports the Reuters news agency.MSF also raised concerns over "excessive concentration" of efforts in certain areas at the expense of other areas where needs were more urgent.It said the response was "too slow" in North Kivu province while Haut-Uélé remained "dramatically overlooked". In both provinces, MSF observed that teams were "inadequately resourced to respond effectively" with health facilities lacking essential items such as water, chlorine or triage systems."This has turned some facilities into new centres of transmission, rather than places of care that contribute to containing the disease," MSF said.

schema.headline: Ebola in DR Congo: Millions of dollars going missing as virus spreads, MSF warns

title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
description: Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry
body: Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded."What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said."Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts. News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion."My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC."I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg."Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital."The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known"."The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths."Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza. Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp. The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City. Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says

title: US envoys head to meet Zelensky after talks with Putin in Moscow
description: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held a fresh round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest discussi
body: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held a fresh round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest discussions aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.The pair are now flying to Dublin to meet Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Witkoff said a new round of trilateral talks had already been agreed with Putin.But in a sign of further tension, Zelensky said on Thursday morning that Ukraine's military was again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.The peace talks in the Emirates were framed as being centred around European security arrangements in a post-war scenario, although a resolution to the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 still appears distant.Comments by both President Vladimir Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.Witkoff said that Europeans would join the next round of talks. "They are our partners and it's important to us that they take part," Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin, but Downing Street later said they had been delayed, meaning the national security adviser could no longer join.Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side but added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going." He did not elaborate further.Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line. A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed and it remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions.Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".Meanwhile, some of the longstanding roadblocks in the peace process were addressed during the US-Russia talks in the Kremlin.The territorial issue continues to be a key point of contention, Putin said. "For us there is only one line of demarcation: the line of the state border. Because then it will be clear that we are here, and you are there. As soon as we start discussing 'grey zones'… arguments immediately start and any agreements become unstable. And there will be no lasting peace."He also suggested organising a humanitarian truce to allow for the evacuation of hundreds of civilians from a frontline area, on the model of last month's ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.Putin suggested a similar five-day ceasefire for Kostyantynivka, a contested front-line Ukrainian city in the eastern region of Donetsk.Kyiv disputes that Russia fully holds the town, and a truce could help Moscow's troops to make a final push to seize it."Considering that they brought in equipment and rotated troops in Oleshky under the guise of a humanitarian operation, it's clear what they want in Kostyantynivka," Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmitry Lytvyn told the BBC, adding that the details would need to be "clarified".But at the core of this week's talks has been the issue of European security architecture. Earlier Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said it was "clear that the current system does not work."Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin and that decisions about their continent could be made without them.Zelensky said he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia "a bit strange"."It is a significant shift in the US position that the US has now taken on board the Russian demand that the European security architecture needs to be discussed and agreed upon in parallel with the Ukraine peace talks," said the Director of the Estonian Foreign Policy Institute Kristi Raik.She said the Russians have a "long history" of wanting to revise European security architecture, intended as core principles "like sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principle that there is no use of force to some conflicts".Russia "has long looked to reduced Nato presence on the Eastern flank and that… get some kind of veto rights in decisions concerning European security and defence," Raik said. "And that's where it gets even more difficult to imagine that there could be an agreement between the Europeans and the Russians." On Thursday, Putin again repeated that the presence of foreign troops in Ukraine was "unacceptable" to Russia, and said Russia would like the Americans to engage with Europe "so that the Europeans can decide what they truly want: peace or war".During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.That position has now shifted for many as concern that decisions about the European continent could be made without European involvement.Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.Top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas told the BBC's Newshour programme the presence of a European official at the next meeting showed the Kremlin had "now realised that Europe is a big player here because we are the ones who have been supporting Ukraine". With financial pressures on European budgets, Kallas said it was "becoming harder to help Ukraine", but warned of the "the danger not only for the eastern flank of the European Union but actually for our whole continent" if Russian aggression was allowed to continue.The Kremlin has not confirmed the make-up of next week's talks, and at the start of the meeting, Putin had indicated he didn't want European countries to play a full role. The Russians have long cited Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle to their involvement.Speaking to Kushner and Witkoff, Putin said he was encouraging them "to work with your European allies so that they finally decide whether they want peace or war in Ukraine."

schema.headline: US envoys head to meet Zelensky after talks with Putin in Moscow

title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
description: Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election. "They did not believ
body: Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election. "They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said."It's not something that I did y'all," he continued. "It's something we did.""In Mississippi, it's local people that make the difference."Dozens of people were gathered at the Mississippi HQ of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Jackson on Wednesday when Colom's victory was announced.The room burst into deafening applause and cheers."This is an amazing result," said Leon Russell, chairman of the NAACP board."This is purely the work of particularly the black community," he continued. "There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organising."This is a historic election."Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory."When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans.Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.The 67-year-old Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. The party flipped Senate seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.

schema.headline: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century

title: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident
description: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of
body: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives."Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding."I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the front line of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.But the workers have a huge task on their hands.Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.Nairobi's drainage system has not been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about seven million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely. But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary. However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers."Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come - or how much rain there will be.But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October-December 2026".So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that is because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall."For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean."We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather - including the risk of both floods and drought.The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

title: Bola Tinubu: Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
description: Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing sho
body: Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms."That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians."Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC. "Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index. However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households."Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness. Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months. Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy."My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities."The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters."These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of  SBM Intelligence.To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult. Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields."They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers."The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria. Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security."Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW."There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment. The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year. Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins."The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say. "Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said."The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said. Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government."APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds."It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said."The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

schema.headline: Bola Tinubu: Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?

title: Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
description: An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father. Koah Sharpe had been missing
body: An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father. Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him. The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery. Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father. The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house. Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah. Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said. He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard". "The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot."The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained. Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show. Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems. "Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

schema.headline: Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina

title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
description: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.Uk
body: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic. Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details."The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace. He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

schema.headline: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland

title: Search for British woman missing from Atlantic cruise suspended
description: The search for a British woman who is believed to have gone overboard from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic has been suspended, the US
body: The search for a British woman who is believed to have gone overboard from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic has been suspended, the US Coast Guard (USCG) has said.The 72-year-old was last seen aboard Tui's Marella Voyager on Monday while the vessel was en route to the Caribbean. Staff realised she was missing on Tuesday, when they noticed her "bed untouched". USCG said the ship was approximately 500 nautical miles from the area where she was believed to entered the water when it received a missing report.It added that a coordinated international search and rescue effort had been called off on Wednesday due to factors including "the low likelihood of survival".USCG said the woman was last recorded accessing a cabin door at about midday on Monday. She is believed to have gone overboard in a remote area of the North Atlantic, roughly 1,400 nautical miles from Bermuda.In a previous statement, Tui said that after staff realised she was missing, the alarm was raised and a search carried out. The Daily Mail earlier reported that holidaymakers on board the ship had been told to abandon dinners, drinks and entertainment as the crew carried out an emergency headcount on Tuesday evening.Passengers stood in lines of four while staff scanned boarding cards to verify the identity of every person on the ship, according to the newspaper.In a statement, USCG confirmed it had received a missing report at about 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) on Tuesday.The coast guard said staff also reported that the Marella did not have enough fuel to return to the search area. It is understood that USCG asked the ship to continue its crossing rather than reverse course and search for the woman.It said that volunteers from the coast guard then worked with search and rescue partners including the Maritime Rescue Coordination Center Delgada and the UK's Joint Rescue Coordination Centre, and issued urgent maritime broadcasts requesting assistance from ships in the area.It added that multiple commercial vessels were contacted as part of the operation to "consider search opportunities, but none were in the vicinity". Search efforts were suspended at about 15:50 EST (20:50 GMT) on Wednesday, "after considering the extensive search area, the elapsed time between the presumed incident and notification, the lack of available search assets in the remote location, negative results from maritime broadcasts, the sea state, and the low likelihood of survival", the coast guard said. The Marella Voyager, carrying around 2,000 passengers and 800 crew, left Malaga on 4 November and is due to arrive in Antigua on Friday before calling at Dominica and finishing its voyage in Barbados on Sunday.A spokeswoman for Marella Cruises earlier said it was supporting the authorities with their enquiries. It added it was "deeply saddened" by the disappearance, adding: "Our thoughts are with the guest's loved ones at this very difficult time.A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said in an earlier statement:  "We are supporting the family of a British national reported missing on a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean and we are in touch with the relevant authorities." In a separate case, a cruise ship pianist was found treading water on Sunday around 20 miles off the Californian coast after falling overboard.Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

schema.headline: Search for British woman missing from Atlantic cruise suspended
